## Body
In 2019, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved the first generic maintenance inhaler for asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) (1). The inhaler, Wixela Inhub (fluticasone-salmeterol, Viatris), is a substitutable version of the dry powder inhaler Advair Diskus (fluticasone-salmeterol, GlaxoSmithKline), which went off-patent in 2016 after becoming the highest selling maintenance inhaler in US history (2,3).
Prior to approving Wixela Inhub, the FDA rejected several earlier applications for generic versions of Advair Diskus, including products from Mylan (4), Hikma (5), and Sandoz (6). Demonstrations of bioequivalence for inhalers have been notoriously difficult given the challenges of measuring regional lung deposition, the complex interactions between the device and active ingredient, and the need for proper technique when using these products (7). To manage this complexity, the FDA applies an “aggregate weight-of-evidence approach” in evaluating generic inhalers, requiring in vitro studies, pharmacokinetic studies, and comparative clinical endpoint or pharmacodynamic studies (7,8).
Despite these rigorous standards, the clinical studies required by the FDA tend to be limited in scope. When approving Wixela Inhub, the FDA permitted the generic firm to complete its comparative clinical endpoint study only in patients with asthma—the most clinically responsive population—even while giving the product labeled indications for both asthma and COPD (9,10). In addition, the pivotal trial of Wixela Inhub analyzed forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) at 28 days rather than clinical effectiveness outcomes (such as respiratory exacerbations) or safety measures (such as episodes of pneumonia) that are often needed for approval of brand-name originators (9). The rationale for requiring less evidence from generic inhaler manufacturers is clear; the active ingredients have already proven safe and effective in clinical trials, and the need to complete more complicated trials could unnecessarily delay competition even further (11).
The end result, however, is that complex drug-device combinations like Wixela Inhub may not have been tested in key populations for whom the product is indicated. The FDA permits small differences in device design between generic and brand-name inhalers so long as user interfaces are similar (12). Such differences could lead to poorer performance of a given product in patients with COPD compared to asthma, as lung deposition of active ingredients delivered via dry powder inhalers may differ across disease states. We therefore used a large, longitudinal healthcare database to analyze the comparative effectiveness and safety of generic vs. brand-name fluticasone-salmeterol in patients with COPD. Regulatory bodies, such as the FDA (13) and European Medicines Agency (14), and professional societies, including the American Thoracic Society (15), have called for well-designed observational studies to inform clinical decision-making and treatment guidelines in situations like the generic Wixela Inhub approval when data from randomized controlled trials are absent, incomplete, or conflicting. Such studies have a particularly important place in COPD given concerns that have been raised about the generalizability of randomized controlled trials, which often exclude patients with extensive co-morbidities and rely on run-in periods that can lead to bias (15,16).

## Methods
Study cohort
This study was performed in Optum’s de-identified Clinformatics® Data Mart (eMethods). Patients were included if they initiated a new (index) prescription for Wixela Inhub (comparator) or Advair Diskus (referent) from January 1, 2018 to June 31, 2021 (eFigure 1). Participants had to be enrolled in the dataset for at least 180 consecutive days prior to cohort entry (the covariate assessment window) and have a diagnosis of COPD, which was defined based on International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision, Clinical Modification (ICD-9-CM) (491.xx, 492.xx, or 496) and ICD-10-CM codes (J41.x, J42, J43.x, J44.x). To indicate active disease, we required patients to have at least 3 outpatient claims or 1 inpatient claim in the prior 3 years (up to and including the index date) for a COPD diagnosis (positive predictive [PPV] 0.82 [95% confidence interval [CI] 0.72-0.89]) (17). We excluded patients who received either the comparator, referent, or any other inhaler from the same therapeutic class—the inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)-long-acting beta agonists (LABA) class—during the covariate assessment window, which included the index date. We also excluded patients under the age of 40 to increase the specificity of the COPD diagnosis. Those who received inhalers other than ICS-LABAs during the baseline period were included in the analysis. However, we excluded patients who initiated triple therapy on the cohort entry date (e.g., receiving a LAMA separately from their ICS-LABA).
Assessment of covariates
We measured potential confounders during the 180 days before (and up to) the cohort entry date (eFigure 1) and included all of the following covariates in our propensity score model: age at cohort entry, sex, race, region, timing of cohort entry (before or during the COVID-19 pandemic), and measures of baseline lung disease. These included the number of baseline moderate COPD exacerbations, number of baseline severe COPD exacerbations, maintenance inhaler therapy, rescue inhaler therapy, chronic oral therapy for COPD [azithromycin, roflumilast, or prednisone], number of pneumonia hospitalizations, filling of antibiotic prescriptions for respiratory infections, home oxygen equipment, CPAP or BiPAP, use of spirometry, smoking, and pulmonary rehabilitation. We also included measures of respiratory events in the 30 days leading up to cohort entry (including moderate or severe COPD exacerbations and use of antibiotics for respiratory infections), baseline eosinophil levels, other co-morbidities (including a combined comorbidity score (18), a frailty index score (19), obstructive sleep apnea, hypertension, diabetes, obesity, coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease, venous thromboembolic disease, congestive heart failure, gastroesophageal reflux disease, renal failure, osteoporosis, dementia or other neurologic disease, malignancy, anxiety disorders, and depression), healthcare utilization during the baseline period (including emergency department visits hospitalizations, 90-day readmissions, office visits, pulmonology office visits, prescription drug claims, basic metabolic or complete metabolic panels, electrocardiograms, echocardiograms, CT scans, bronchoscopies, colonoscopies, mammography, bone-mineral density scans, and influenza vaccination), and non-pulmonary medications (statins, beta-blockers, angiotensin-converting enzyme-inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, calcium channel blockers, thiazide diuretics, loop diuretics, proton-pump inhibitors, H2-receptor blockers, metformin, sulfonylureas, sodium-glucose co-transporter [SGLT2] inhibitors, dipeptidyl peptidase-4 [DPP-4] inhibitors, combination SGLT2-DPP-4 inhibitors, benzodiazepines, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors or serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors). We measured cost-related covariates during the covariate assessment window while excluding the day of cohort entry (mean copayment, total copayment, and ratio of unique brand-name to generic drugs), and we assessed whether patients ever had diagnosis codes for asthma using all available time in the dataset. We determined whether index prescriptions were written by a pulmonologist (vs. other type of provider) on the cohort entry date.
Outcomes and follow-up
The primary effectiveness outcome was time to first moderate or severe COPD exacerbation beginning the day after cohort entry. Moderate COPD exacerbations were defined as requiring prednisone for 5-14 days (PPV 0.73) (20), and severe COPD exacerbations were defined as requiring hospitalization (with COPD in the primary position using the codes specified above for defining COPD) (PPV 0.86) (21). Episodes that met both moderate and severe exacerbation criteria within 14 days of each other were counted as one severe exacerbation that began at the time of meeting the criteria for the first exacerbation within the episode, regardless of whether the criteria were for a moderate or severe exacerbation. The distinction between moderate COPD exacerbations requiring oral steroids and severe COPD exacerbations requiring hospitalization has been widely used in clinical guidelines (22), randomized controlled trials (23-25), and other claims-based studies (26-32).
The primary safety outcome was time to first hospitalization for pneumonia (ICD-10-CM J09.X1, J10.xx-J18.x, A01.03, A02.22, A37.01, A37.11 A37.81, A37.91, A54.84, B01.2, B05.2, B06.81, B77.81, J85.1, J22). The codes for pneumonia hospitalizations have been validated with a PPV of 0.88 using ICD-9 codes; we converted ICD-9 to ICD-10 codes based on clinical review (33).
We followed patients for up to one year after cohort entry or until any of the following occurred: discontinuation of index therapy (with a 60-day grace period between refills), a switch from exposure to referent or vice-versa, the addition of a LAMA, initiation of another ICS-LABA, initiation of a LAMA-LABA, initiation of an ICS-LAMA-LABA, death, the end of insurance coverage, or the end of data. We censored patients at treatment discontinuation or switch, because our primary analysis was an on-treatment analysis.
Statistical analysis
We used 1:1 propensity score matching to adjust for confounding between the two treatment groups using nearest neighbor matching without replacement and a caliper of 0.01 on the propensity scale. We included all covariates in Table 1 in the propensity score model, and users were matched in rank order based on their propensity scores. When data were missing for a covariate, we used a missing indicator in our propensity score model. We estimated propensity scores using logistic regression, and we estimated hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% CIs using a Cox proportional hazards regression model.
We performed a range of prespecified secondary, subgroup, and sensitivity analyses. Secondary analyses included the incidence of first moderate COPD exacerbation and first severe COPD exacerbation (analyzed separately), the annual rate of total moderate or severe COPD exacerbations (analyzed separately and together), and the annual rate of total pneumonia hospitalizations. When assessing annual rates of COPD exacerbations and pneumonia hospitalizations, we used a Poisson model, and we required that distinct episodes of exacerbations be separated by at least 14 days.
Subgroup analyses included patients with one or more baseline moderate or severe COPD exacerbations in the 180 days before cohort entry, those with one or more severe COPD exacerbations in the 180 days before cohort entry, those with no prior asthma diagnoses, those who received their index prescription before the COVID-19 pandemic, those who underwent spirometry before cohort entry, and those whose index prescription was written by a pulmonologist. All subgroup analyses were performed both in patients who met the criteria specified above and the remainder who did not. For subgroup analyses, propensity scores within each subgroup were re-estimated and patients were re-matched. In one subgroup analysis (those enrolled during the COVID-19 pandemic), there were insufficient numbers for re-estimating the propensity score and re-matching. Therefore, we performed this analysis by splitting the overall 1:1 matched cohort into subgroups and analyzed them without re-matching.
We performed prespecified sensitivity analyses to assess the robustness of our findings. We conducted an analysis using 1:1 high-dimensional propensity score matching, which adjusts for hundreds of empirically defined covariates using an automated algorithm based on ICD-10 diagnosis codes and procedure codes for inpatient confinements and medical services, Current Procedure Terminology codes for medical services, and prescription drug claims (based on National Drug Code generic name) (34-36). We also varied the grace period permitted between prescription fills during follow up (to 30 days and 90 days) and excluded the first 30 days and first 60 days after cohort entry when assessing outcomes. We conducted an intention-to-treat analysis in which patients were followed irrespective of treatment discontinuation or switching (unlike the primary on-treatment analysis, in which patients were censored at treatment discontinuation or switch). In separate sensitivity analyses, we varied the definition of moderate exacerbation: (1) to require an office or emergency department visit before the prednisone fill; (2) to require both a prednisone and antibiotic fill on the same day; and (3) to permit either a prednisone or an antibiotic fill on the same day. We also varied the definitions of severe exacerbation (to permit a COPD exacerbation code in any position) and pneumonia hospitalization (to require the diagnosis code in the primary position). In a post-hoc sensitivity analysis, we used inverse-probability-of-censoring weights to estimate a different estimand from the primary on-treatment analysis or the intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis.
The complete protocol for this study was preregistered at the Center for Open Science Real World Evidence Registry (available at https://osf.io/v89qz). The study was approved by the Mass General Brigham Institutional Review Board.
Funding
This research was funded by a grant from the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (K08HL163246) to Dr. Feldman. Drs. Kesselheim, Avorn, and Feldman also receive funding from the Commonwealth Fund and Arnold Ventures. The funders had no role in the design, conduct, or analysis of the study or in the decision to submit the manuscript for publication.

## Results
The overall cohort included 45,369 patients, of whom 18,064 patients received Wixela Inhub and 27,305 patients received Advair Diskus (Figure 1; Table 1). Patients receiving Wixela Inhub tended to be older (mean age 72.7 vs. 70.8) but have slightly fewer baseline moderate COPD exacerbations (mean 0.29 vs. 0.30), baseline severe COPD exacerbations (mean 0.04 vs. 0.05), baseline fills of short-acting beta agonist rescue inhalers (mean 1.14 vs. 1.19), and baseline fills of respiratory antibiotics (0.78 vs. 0.88). Because of increased generic uptake towards the end of our study, a higher proportion of patients who received Wixela Inhub filled their index prescription during the COVID-19 pandemic (60.5%) compared to patients who initiated Advair Diskus (10.5%).
Matches were found for 10,012 pairs in the cohort. The groups were well balanced after matching, including for index prescription during the COVID-19 pandemic (28.8% in the exposure group vs. 29.1% in the referent group). The characteristics of the propensity-score matched cohort and absolute standardized differences are presented alongside the overall cohort in Table 1. The pre- and post-matching distributions of propensity score overlap are presented in eFigure 2.
Primary effectiveness and safety endpoints
There were 2,793 first moderate or severe COPD exacerbations among patients in the matched cohort during 6,618 person-years of follow-up, giving a crude incidence of 422.0 events per 1,000 person-years. The hazard ratio (HR) for first moderate or severe COPD exacerbation was similar for patients who received Wixela Inhub compared to patients who received Advair Diskus (HR 0.97, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.90-1.04) (Table 2). The absolute rate was similar between the two groups (rate difference: −24.9 events per 1,000 person years [95% CI −122.3-72.5 events per 1,000 person-years]). Median follow-up time was 88 days (interquartile range [IQR] 66-148) for patients receiving Wixela Inhub and 88 days (IQR 61-148) for those receiving Advair Diskus.
Seven hundred and thirty patients in the matched cohort experienced the primary safety outcome of first pneumonia hospitalization during 7,165 person-years of follow-up (crude incidence 101.9 events per 1,000 person-years). The hazard ratio (HR 0.99 [95% CI 0.86-1.15]) and absolute rate of first pneumonia hospitalization (−3.44 events per 1,000 person-years [95% CI −56.2-49.3 events per 1,000 person-years) were similar between the two groups. Median follow-up time was 101 days (IQR 88-167 days) for patients receiving Wixela Inhub and 88 days (IQR 79-148 days) for those receiving Advair Diskus.
The reasons for censoring for the primary effectiveness and safety outcomes are given in eTable 1 and eTable 2. Sensitivity analyses for the primary effectiveness outcome and primary safety outcome resulted in similar findings to the primary analysis (Figure 2; eFigure 3).
Moderate vs. severe COPD exacerbations
When analyzing the components of the primary endpoint separately, Wixela Inhub was associated with a similar hazard of first moderate COPD exacerbation as Advair Diskus (HR 0.96 [95% CI 0.89-1.04]) and a similar hazard of first severe COPD exacerbation (HR 1.04 [95% CI 0.84-1.29]). Sensitivity analyses, presented in eFigure 4 and eFigure 5, show similar findings.
Total moderate or severe COPD exacerbations and total pneumonia hospitalizations
Patients in the matched cohort had a total of 3,861 moderate or severe COPD exacerbations (including recurrent events) during 8,016 person-years of follow-up (crude incidence of 481.7 events per 1,000 person-years) and a total of 986 total pneumonia hospitalizations (crude incidence of 123.0 events per 1,000 person-years). Those receiving Wixela Inhub had similar rates of total moderate or severe COPD exacerbations (incident rate ratio [IRR] 0.96, 95% CI 0.90-1.02) and similar rates of total pneumonia hospitalization (IRR 0.98, 95% CI 0.86-1.11).
Subgroup analysis
Wixela Inhub was not associated with a higher incidence of first moderate or severe COPD exacerbation than Advair Diskus for any subgroup in our analysis, including those with higher COPD severity (based on prior exacerbations) or who lacked an asthma diagnosis codes in their record (Figure 3). Likewise, no differences were observed in the incidence of first pneumonia hospitalization for any subgroup studied (eFigure 6).

## Discussion
The first generic maintenance inhaler to receive FDA approval, Wixela Inhub, was associated with similar rates of first moderate or severe COPD exacerbation and similar rates of first pneumonia hospitalization as the brand-name reference drug, Advair Diskus, in a population of patients with COPD treated in routine clinical care. These findings were robust across a range of prespecified secondary, sensitivity, and subgroup analyses. Our study adds important new data supporting the clinical equivalence of generic and brand-name fluticasone-salmeterol in a group of patients who were not included in clinical trials leading to Wixela Inhub approval.
Fluticasone-salmeterol and other ICS-LABAs remain widely prescribed for patients with COPD. However, treatment guidelines have evolved in recent years to favor other maintenance regimens. A large randomized controlled trial in 2016 showed that patients receiving LAMA-LABA therapy had fewer COPD exacerbations and fewer episodes of pneumonia than patients receiving ICS-LABA therapy (23). The 2017 Global Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) guidelines began recommending LAMA-LABA over ICS-LABA therapy except in patients with frequent exacerbations, high eosinophil counts, or co-occurring asthma (37), and the 2023 GOLD guidelines replaced ICS-LABAs altogether with triple therapy (ICS-LAMA-LABA) when patients required an inhaled corticosteroid (22).
These recent shifts in the GOLD guidelines raise the question about the role of ICS-LABAs like fluticasone-salmeterol in the management of COPD. Yet, studies assessing the clinical equivalence of generic vs. brand-name fluticasone-salmeterol remain vital for several reasons. First, these inhalers have an FDA-approved indication for COPD, and rates of ICS-LABA prescribing have remained persistently high despite guideline-changes (38,39). When a physician prescribes Advair Diskus, pharmacists may automatically substitute Wixela Inhub (regardless of the indication) (40). Evidence supporting the therapeutic equivalence of generic ICS-LABAs for use in COPD thus remains valuable given actual prescribing patterns.
In addition, many patients who receive triple therapy according to the GOLD guidelines may receive this therapy via two separate inhalers—an ICS-LABA and a LAMA inhaler. Combined ICS-LAMA-LABA inhalers are expensive (41), with only 2 approved brand-name versions and no generics on the US market (2). While the GOLD guidelines favor minimizing the number of inhalers a patient must use, the guidelines also recognize the effects of high costs on patient access and adherence (22). The two brand-name ICS-LAMA-LABAs on the US market have patents extending into the 2030s (2). With generic LAMAs poised to enter the market before then, clinicians may face the difficult choice of prescribing an expensive combined brand-name ICS-LAMA-LABA inhaler or separate generic ICS-LABA and LAMA inhalers, which may lower the costs for patients and payers and increase affordability (2). The ease of using a single inhaler may boost adherence, but excess out-of-pocket spending could counteract and even outweigh these benefits in some patients. Evidence supporting the effectiveness and safety of generic ICS-LABAs can help promote less expensive options for patients with COPD who require an inhaled corticosteroid as part of their regimen.
Finally, this study illustrates the utility of real-world post-marketing studies comparing complex generic products to brand-name referents, which are faster and less expensive than mounting new randomized clinical trials to test for equivalence and which can study drug effects in large numbers of typical patients receiving routine care. Such post-marketing studies should strengthen the confidence of regulators, clinicians, payers, and professional societies in FDA standards for bioequivalence. Our findings support the FDA’s conclusion of clinical equivalence in the case of Wixela Inhub and produce complementary evidence for the trial that was required by the FDA, which analyzed only patients with asthma and assessed a surrogate endpoint (FEV1) (11). We believe that post-marketing studies among patients using generic drug-device combinations during clinical care should be routine for regulatory bodies after approval. Any concerning findings may then prompt further investigation by the FDA, including the possibility of additional clinical trials. A willingness by the FDA to rely on post-marketing studies to assess such products could also permit further flexibility to expedite generic approvals.
Several limitations to our analysis should be noted. First, while we adjusted for many covariates, we cannot exclude the possibility of residual confounding. Of particular concern is the fact that a large proportion of Wixela Inhub users initiated therapy during the COVID-19 pandemic, as generic uptake increased following approval in 2019. However, our primary propensity-score matched analysis included an equal number of patients in each treatment group who received their index prescription before vs. during the COVID-19 pandemic. In addition, subgroup analyses showed that patients who initiated Wixela or Advair Diskus before the pandemic had similar outcomes; the same was true of initiators during the COVID-19 pandemic. Second, follow-up times were short in the study, reflecting experience in clinical practice in which patients often discontinue their inhaler therapy. Reassuringly, our intention-to-treat analysis yielded similar findings to the primary analysis. We sought to further address questions of informative censoring in a post-hoc inverse-probability-of-censoring weighted analysis; however, we do not have good predictors of censoring, which limits our ability to effectively address informative censoring. Third, while pneumonia is considered perhaps the most important safety risk of ICS-LABA therapy, there are other safety risks, such as oral thrush, that we did not assess. Fourth, our analysis assumes that patients who filled their prescriptions for generic and brand-name fluticasone-salmeterol inhalers used the therapy as prescribed and that there was no differential misuse between the comparator and referent groups. Fifth, our analysis was restricted to the first interchangeable generic substitute for Advair Diskus, Wixela Inhub. We did not consider more recently approved generic fluticasone-salmeterol inhalers. Sixth, the population in our study consists of patients with insurance coverage through United HealthCare. While this dataset includes millions of covered lives across all 50 states, replication of our analysis in other patient populations, particularly those with Medicare plans, may help further validate our findings.

## Conclusion
In patients with COPD, the generic ICS-LABA Wixela Inhub had nearly identical effectiveness and safety when compared to brand-name Advair Diskus. Similar studies can provide a useful means of evaluating the clinical effectiveness and safety of complex generic products after approval.

title: The effect of bradykinin 1 receptor antagonist BI 1026706 on pulmonary inflammation after segmental lipopolysaccharide challenge in healthy smokers.
body:
BACKGROUND: Bradykinin 1 receptor (B1R) signalling pathways may be involved in the inflammatory pathophysiology of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). B1R signalling is induced by inflammatory stimuli or tissue injury and leads to activation and increased migration of pro-inflammatory cells. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) lung challenge in man is an experimental method of exploring inflammation in the lung whereby interference in these pathways can help to assess pharmacologic interventions in COPD. BI 1026706, a potent B1R antagonist, was hypothesized to reduce the inflammatory activity after segmental lipopolysaccharide (LPS) challenge in humans due to decreased pulmonary cell influx.
METHODS: In a monocentric, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, phase I trial, 57 healthy, smoking subjects were treated for 28 days with either oral BI 1026706 100 mg bid or placebo. At day 21, turbo-inversion recovery magnitude magnetic resonance imaging (TIRM MRI) was performed. On the last day of treatment, pre-challenge bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BAL) and biopsies were sampled, followed by segmental LPS challenge (40 endotoxin units/kg body weight) and saline control instillation in different lung lobes. Twenty-four hours later, TIRM MRI was performed, then BAL and biopsies were collected from the challenged segments. In BAL samples, cells were differentiated for neutrophil numbers as the primary endpoint. Other endpoints included assessment of safety, biomarkers in BAL (e.g. interleukin-8 [IL-8], albumin and total protein), B1R expression in lung biopsies and TIRM score by MRI as a measure for the extent of pulmonary oedema.
RESULTS: After LPS, but not after saline, high numbers of inflammatory cells, predominantly neutrophils were observed in the airways. IL-8, albumin and total protein were also increased in BAL samples after LPS challenge as compared with saline control. There were no significant differences in cells or other biomarkers from BAL in volunteers treated with BI 1026706 compared with those treated with placebo. Unexpectedly, neutrophil numbers in BAL were 30% higher and MRI-derived extent of oedema was significantly higher with BI 1026706 treatment compared with placebo, 24 h after LPS challenge. Adverse events were mainly mild to moderate and not different between treatment groups.
CONCLUSIONS: Treatment with BI 1026706 for four weeks was safe and well-tolerated in healthy smoking subjects. BI 1026706 100 mg bid did not provide evidence for anti-inflammatory effects in the human bronchial LPS challenge model.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: The study was registered on January 14, 2016 at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT02657408).

title: The Effect of Albuterol Spray on Hypoxia and Bronchospasm in Patients with Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) under General Anesthesia: A bouble-Blind Randomized Clinical Trial.
body:
BACKGROUND: Patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) experience an increased risk of perioperative pulmonary complications. The aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of albuterol spray on hypoxia and bronchospasm in patients with COPD under general anesthesia.
METHODS: This single-center, double-blind, parallel-group, randomized clinical trial was performed on 120 smoking patients with COPD who were referred to 5 Azar Educational Hospital in Gorgan, Northern Iran, in 2021. Twenty minutes before general anesthesia and also after completion of surgery and before extubation, 60 patients in the intervention group were inhaled with 2 puffs of albuterol spray. In the control group, patients were inhaled with 2 puffs of placebo spray. In perioperative period, the occurrence of wheezing, bronchospasm, coughing, hemodynamic changes, postoperative shivering, dyspnea, and nausea and vomiting were evaluated in all patients. The Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) checklist was used to report important aspects of this study.
RESULTS: The mean age of the patients was 52.34 ±8.95 years, and 115 (95.8%) of them were males while the rest were females. The difference between systolic blood pressure before induction of anesthesia (after administration of albuterol spray) between the group receiving albuterol spray and the group not receiving it was statistically significant (p=0.04). Also, the difference between the mean arterial oxygen saturation before tracheal extubation (after re-administration of albuterol spray) between the albuterol spray group and the non-albuterol group was statistically significant (p = 0.03). Wheezing and recurrent cough after induction of anesthesia and after extubation (after albuterol spray administration) was lower in the albuterol group than in the control group (p<0.05). No significant side effects were detected in the albuterol-treated group.
CONCLUSION: According to the results of this study, it seems that the prophylactic use of albuterol spray is useful in reducing the incidence of wheezing and recurrent cough before induction of anesthesia in COPD patients with smoking.

## Introduction
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a common chronic disease, third leading cause of death and increasingly important cause of morbidity and disability in the world. It is characterized by poorly reversible and progressive airflow obstruction (1). Genetic and environmental risk factors such as exposure to tobacco smoke, indoor air pollution and occupational dusts, fumes and chemicals are important risk factors for COPD (2). Among the multiple risk factors, cigarette smoking is the strongest risk factor for COPD. Carbon monoxide in cigarette smoke has 200-300 times greater affinity for hemoglobin than oxygen and produces carboxyhemoglobin, leading to tissue hypoxia (3). Considering that many of COPD patents will need surgery and general anesthesia during their lives, these patients should be evaluated for hypoxia, bronchospasm, and laryngospasm in perioperative period by conducting a thorough clinical history and physical examination and performing pulmonary function testing (PFT) and arterial blood gases (ABG) analysis (4,5).
Patients with COPD pose a challenge to the anesthesiologists because intraoperative and postoperative complications occur more commonly in these patients, which can lead to prolonged hospital stay and increased mortality (6). Therefore, it is important to take proper measures to reduce the incidence of postoperative pulmonary complications to improve the quality of surgical care and reduce the medical cost (6,7).
Inhaled bronchodilators such as albuterol, a short acting β agonist, are widely prescribed for the symptomatic relief in patients with COPD. Beta-2 adrenergic receptor agonists (β2-agonists) can result in bronchodilatation by stimulating the β2-adrenoceptor present on airway smooth muscle and other cells in the airway (8). Albuterol can often decrease symptoms of airflow obstruction by bronchodilatation, decreasing dyspnea, and improving quality of life (9,10).
Previously, it has been shown that using prophylactic salbutamol spray before surgery, reduces the incidence of bronchospasm and coughing in heavy smoking patients under general anesthesia (11). Also, it has been indicated that using salbutamol aerosol decreases the occurrence of postoperative bronchospasm and pulmonary infiltration in patients with mild-to-moderate COPD (12). However, there is limited evidence regarding the efficacy of perioperative inhaled albuterol on hypoxia and bronchospasms in COPD patients who underwent elective surgeries using general anesthesia. Therefore, the aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of albuterol spray on hypoxia and bronchospasm in patients with COPD under general anesthesia. We hypothesized that using perioperative albuterol spray would reduce hypoxia and bronchospasm in patients with COPD under general anesthesia.

## Methods
In a double-blind randomized clinical trial, after obtaining review and obtaining adequate permissions from the University's Ethics Committee and informed consent from patients, 120 patients who were a candidate for elective surgeries under general anesthesia at 5 Azar Educational Hospital in Gorgan, Iran, were recruited, in 2021.
Patients with previously confirmed diagnosis of COPD, class I or II of American Society of Anesthesiologists, aged between 18 and 65 years and had history of cigarette smoking were included. The exclusion criteria were patients' unwillingness to participate or discontinue the study at any time during the study period, prolongation of surgery duration (more than 3 hours), cardiac dysfunction or heart failure, intraoperative blood loss and the need for transfusion, allergy to salbutamol preparations, smoking cigarettes during 12 hours before surgery, exacerbation of COPD, concomitant pulmonary arterial hypertension (defined as a mean pulmonary arterial pressure > 25 mmHg) and hemodynamic changes >20% from the baseline (blood pressure, heart rate and reduction in SpO2) that need to be managed.
Patients who fulfilled the inclusion criteria were randomly allocated using block randomization method to two equally sized groups of A and B (n=60) by a nurse anesthetist. For ensuring allocation concealment, the sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelope technique was used by a nurse who was unaware of the study groups.
In the operating room, all patients were connected to electrocardiography, peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2) and non-invasive blood pressure monitor and all the basal parameters were recorded. All patients were placed under general anesthesia using a similar anesthetic protocol including midazolam (0.02 mg/kg), fentanyl (3-5 µ/kg), lidocaine (1 mg/kg), propofol (2 mg/kg) nesdonal (5 mg/kg) and cisatracurium (0.2 mg/kg) to facilitate endotracheal intubation. After 3 minutes, patients were intubated with appropriate sized cuffed endotracheal tube and administered a mixture of 50% nitrous oxide (N2O), oxygen, and isoflore 1.5 MAC for maintenance of anesthesia. The continuous mandatory ventilation (CMV) mode was initiated after placing the tracheal tube.
Twenty minutes before anesthesia, patients in the group A were administered two puffs of albuterol (2 X 100 micrograms) orally via a metered-dose inhaler, whereas those in the control group (group B) were given a placebo spray in the same way. Also, the shape of the placebo spray was the same as the albuterol spray. After completion of surgery, patients in group A (n=60) received two puffs of albuterol via the endotracheal tube, whereas those in the control group (group B) were given a placebo spray in the same way. At the end of surgery after discontinuation of anesthetic medications, neostigmine 0.04 mg/kg and atropine 0.02 mg/kg were used for muscle relaxant reversal.
Primary and secondary outcomes measure: A lung auscultation was performed to assess wheezing, before administration of albuterol spray and 20 minutes later (after endotracheal intubation), by an anesthesiology resident who was blinded to the study groups. The diagnosis of bronchospasm, during anesthesia, was based on the feel of anesthesiologist that the reservoir bag was too tight when squeezing it (tight bag), in addition to significant depressed SpO2 values. During emergence, coughing was observed and recorded by the same resident blinded to the study protocol and the anesthesia regimen. Patients' systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, mean arterial blood pressure and heart rate were measured and recorded (during surgery every 10 minutes and during 1 hour recovery period every 15 minutes). Also, occurrence of postoperative shivering, dyspnea, and nausea and vomiting were evaluated in patients.
Sample size: A priori sample size were calculated using GPower3.1 with the formula for calculation of samples of repeated measures, based on a presumed effect size of 0.2, a statistical power of 80%, and a type I error of 5%. The overall proper sample size was found to be 108 participants. We therefore recruited 120 patients to account for any dropouts.
Statistical analysis: After data collection, statistical analysis was performed using descriptive and inferential statistics via Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) software (version 18.0, SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). Shapiro-Wilk test was used to assess normality of the data. Chi-Square/Fisher exact test and t-test were used for qualitative and quantitative variables, respectively. A P-value less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) checklist was used to report important aspects of this study.
Ethical considerations: The present study was carried out in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and after the approval of the Institutional Ethics Committee (code: IR.GOUMS.REC.1400.272). The researchers explained the objectives of the study to the participants, and informed consent was obtained from all participants. Also, the protocol of this study was registered in the Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials Database (IRCT20170108031818N1).
Data sharing: All relevant data and methodological details pertaining to this study are available to any interested researchers upon reasonable request to the corresponding author.

## Results
In this study, 133 patients in 5-Azar Hospital in Gorgan were evaluated in terms of inclusion and exclusion criteria. Eight patients did not meet the inclusion criteria while 5 patients did not agree to participate in the study. One hundred twenty patients were randomly assigned to the two groups of A and B in a 1:1 ratio. Finally, all the 120 subjects were evaluated in two groups of intervention and placebo (Figure 1).
The mean age of patients was 52.34±8.95 years, and 115 (95.8%) of them were males. There was no significant difference between the two groups in terms of age and sex. All surgeries in this study were lower extremity and pelvic surgeries.
As shown in Table 1, the difference in systolic blood pressure before induction of anesthesia (after albuterol spray administration) between the group that received albuterol spray and the group that did not receive it was statistically significant (P=0.04). The mean difference of mean arterial blood pressure before anesthesia induction (after administration of albuterol spray) and before tracheal extubation (after re-administration of albuterol spray) between the two groups were statistically significant. Also, the difference in mean of SPO2 before tracheal extubation (after re-administration of albuterol spray) between the two groups were statistically significant (P=0.03).
As shown in Table 2, respiratory wheezing and frequent coughing before anesthesia induction (after albuterol spray administration) were less in the intervention group (receiving albuterol spray) than the control group. However in terms of other symptoms such as bronchospasm, nausea, vomiting, dyspnea and shivering, there was no significant difference between the two groups (P>0.05).
According to the results of the chi-square test before induction of anesthesia, out of 60 patients who received albuterol spray, 5 patients (8.3%) had wheezing, but in the control group, 18 patients (30%) had wheezing (p=0.003). Also, before induction of anesthesia, none of the 60 patients who received albuterol spray had frequent cough, but in the control group, 4 patients (6.7%) had frequent cough (p=0.04). As shown in Table 3, wheezing and bronchospasm before tracheal extubation (after re-administration of albuterol spray) were lower in the intervention group (receiving albuterol spray) than in the control group. However, other symptoms such as frequent cough, nausea, dyspnea, and shivering were not statistically significantly different between the two groups (p>0.05). Before tracheal extubation, out of 60 patients who received albuterol spray, 16 (26.7%) had wheezing, but in the control group, 25 patients (41.7%) had wheezing (P = 0.04). Also, before tracheal extubation, none of the 60 patients who received albuterol spray had bronchospasm, but in the control group, 5 patients (8.3%) had bronchospasm (P=0.01). No significant side effects were detected in the albuterol-treated group.

## Discussion
The results of the present study showed that wheezing and frequent coughing before induction of anesthesia (after administration of albuterol spray) in the intervention group (receiving albuterol spray) were less in the intervention group than the control group. Also, wheezing and bronchospasm before tracheal extubation (after re-administration of albuterol spray) were less in the intervention group than in the control group.
A study by Etamadi et al. showed that out of 30 heavy smoking patients during general anesthesia who received salbutamol spray, 21 had no problems, and only 9 patients from this group had bronchospasm or wheezing or irritating cough or decreased oxygen saturation. Also, out of 30 patients in the control group, 13 were without complications while 17 patients of this group had one or more complications such as bronchospasm, wheezing, irritating cough, and depressed blood oxygen saturation, which were resolved with the necessary medical measures. None of the patients had acute respiratory distress syndrome after surgery (11).
In the study of Imantalab et al. on 225 heavy smoking patients who had a history of smoking (20 packs/year) with normal spirometry and without any respiratory symptoms, who underwent coronary artery bypass surgery, patients were divided into 3 groups (75 in each group).
In the first group were the smoking patients who had not been treated and had smoked before the surgery. The second group consisted of smoking patients who were treated with 3 drugs, Salbutamol-Atronet-Beclomethasone, inhaled 2 puffs twice a day, 10 to 14 days before the surgery, and they had smoked before the operation. In the third group were smokers who had quit smoking for 8 weeks. In the first, second and third groups, out of 75 patients, 35, 23 and 31 suffered from at least one postoperative complications. The frequency of coughing and wheezing and the average duration of mechanical ventilation and the incidence of reoperation due to repeated coughing in the group that was treated with salbutamol-atronate-beclomethasone were statistically lower than the other two groups (13).
Smoking is a major trigger of chronic mucus hyper-secretion, decreases the protective host responses to infection, impairs the capability of cilia to clear mucus and causes air flow obstruction. Also, due to the occurrence of hypoxia in these patients, pulmonary vascular resistance and blood viscosity increase (14,15).
Ninety percent of smoking patients have chronic arterial insufficiency. Although patients are advised for cessation of smoking 8 to 12 weeks before elective surgery or at least 18 hours before surgery, it is observed that these patients continue their smoking habit. The harmful substances in cigarette smoke are not fully known. Some of these substances produce bronchitis in the trachea and large bronchi, and others cause emphysema in smaller bronchioles and alveoli (16–19). In these patients, when chronic airway obstruction occurs, lung damage is irreversible and smoking is the leading cause of COPD. In the pre-operative visit of smoking and COPD patients, the severity of the disease and the possibility of bronchospasm and infection should be evaluated (6,19).
Albuterol is a β2 agonist whose possible mechanisms of action include relaxation of bronchial smooth muscles, stimulation of mucociliary clearance, stabilization of mesenteries, reduction of edema caused by increased vascular permeability, reduction of pulmonary artery pressure, improvement of diaphragm contraction and inhibition of transmission of parasympathetic ganglia in the airways. Beta-agonists have antitussive effects, due to the drug's effect on endothelial and epithelial permeability, inhibiting the release of mediators, and stimulating mucociliary clearance (20,21).
The results of a study by Kim, Eun et al., who investigated the effects of albuterol administration before intubation on the emergence coughing are inconsistent with the present study. In that study, the researchers concluded that emergence coughing is very common, and smoking has no effect on cough during emergence from anesthesia. Also, using albuterol has no beneficial effect on emergence coughing (22). One possible explanation for this inconsistency may be using albuterol spray before intubation and extubation in our study, compared to using albuterol only before intubation in Euns Kim et al's study.
Also, in the study of Hurwitz et al. it was shown that smoking reduced the function of pulmonary vessels and airways, so that albuterol consumption did not cause a significant decrease in pulmonary vascular resistance in both smoking and non-smoking groups. However on the other hand, it caused a greater decrease in airway vascular resistance in non-smokers than in smokers (23). The results of another study by Ramgolam et al. showed that premedication with salbutamol to children aged between 6 and 16 years and at high risk of perioperative respiratory, adverse events including bronchospasm, laryngospasm, airway obstruction, desaturation, coughing and stridor, did not reduce their risk of these adverse events (24). However, the results of another study confirmed the efficacy of albuterol premedication administration before tonsillectomy under general anesthesia in young children in reduction of rates of perioperative respiratory adverse events compared to the rates in children who received placebo (25).
There were some limitations to our study. We did not assess some potential confounders in this study such as preoperative anxiety. Moreover, determining the exact dosage of albuterol that reached the bronchus under the administration of metered-dose inhaler was difficult. In addition, the absence of preoperative pulmonary function data was another limitation of this study.
In conclusion, according to the results of the preset study, it seems that using one puff of albuterol spray (2.5 micrograms) before induction of anesthesia can significantly reduce wheezing and frequent coughing in COPD patients under general anesthesia. Also, re-administration of one puff of albuterol spray (2.5 micrograms) before tracheal extubation can significantly reduce wheezing and bronchospasm compared to the control group. In other words, the preventive use of albuterol spray will be useful in reducing the incidence of bronchospasm and hypoxia, and frequent coughing after anesthesia in COPD patients who smoke.

title: Efficacy and safety of aclidinium/formoterol versus monotherapies and aclidinium versus placebo in Chinese and other Asian patients with moderate-to-severe COPD: The AVANT Phase 3 study.
body: AVANT was a Phase 3, 24-week, randomized, parallel-group, double-blind, double-dummy, placebo-controlled study to assess the efficacy and safety of aclidinium/formoterol 400 μg/12 μg combination vs monotherapies and aclidinium vs placebo (1:1:1:1) in Asian patients (∼70% of whom were Chinese) with moderate-to-severe stable chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Endpoints were analyzed hierarchically to incorporate type I error control. At Week 24, aclidinium/formoterol demonstrated improvements from baseline in 1-h morning post-dose forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1) vs aclidinium (least squares [LS] mean 92 mL; 95% confidence interval [CI] 60, 124 mL; p < 0.001), and in trough FEV1 vs formoterol (LS mean 85 mL; 95% CI 53, 117 mL; p < 0.001). Furthermore, aclidinium provided improvements in trough FEV1 vs placebo (LS mean 134 mL; 95% CI 103, 166 mL; p < 0.001). There was an improvement in transition dyspnea index focal score at Week 24 for aclidinium/formoterol vs placebo (LS mean 0.8; 95% CI 0.2, 1.3; p = 0.005) but not for aclidinium vs placebo (LS mean 0.4; 95% CI -0.1, 1.0; p = 0.132). Improvements in St George's Respiratory Questionnaire total scores occurred for aclidinium/formoterol vs placebo (LS mean -4.0; 95% CI -6.7, -1.4; p = 0.003) and aclidinium vs placebo (LS mean -2.9; 95% CI -5.5, -0.3; p = 0.031). Aclidinium/formoterol and aclidinium were well tolerated and safety findings were consistent with known profiles; rates of treatment-emergent adverse events (AEs) (aclidinium/formoterol: 54.8%; aclidinium: 47.4%; placebo: 53.9%), serious AEs (7.2, 7.9, and 7.8%, respectively), and AEs leading to discontinuation of study medication (2.3, 1.5, and 2.2%, respectively) were similar between groups.

## Abstract
AVANT was a Phase 3, 24-week, randomized, parallel-group, double-blind, double-dummy, placebo-controlled study to assess the efficacy and safety of aclidinium/formoterol 400 μg/12 μg combination vs monotherapies and aclidinium vs placebo (1:1:1:1) in Asian patients (~70% of whom were Chinese) with moderate-to-severe stable chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Furthermore, aclidinium provided improvements in trough FEV1 vs placebo (LS mean 134 mL; 95% CI 103, 166 mL; p < 0.001). There was an improvement in transition dyspnea index focal score at Week 24 for aclidinium/ formoterol vs placebo (LS mean 0.8; 95% CI 0.2, 1.3; p = 0.005) but not for aclidinium vs placebo (LS mean 0.4; 95% CI −0.1, 1.0; p = 0.132). ## Introduction
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a preventable and treatable disease characterized by persistent respiratory symptoms and progressive airflow limitation, which cause substantial impairment of patients’ daily activities and a loss of work productivity [1,2]. Moreover, it is the third leading cause of death worldwide (3.2 million deaths in 2019) [3]. The severity of COPD is assessed by the degree of airflow limitation, impairment of exercise tolerance/physical activity, intensity of dyspnea, and frequency/severity of exacerbations [1]. Early diagnosis and treatment, including smoking cessation, are needed to slow progression of symptoms and prevent exacerbations [4]. A 2019 systematic review of MEDLINE, Embase, Global Health, CINAHL, and Google Scholar found that among people aged 30–79 years, the highest prevalence of COPD was in the Western Pacific (11.7%) and South-East Asian regions (11.6%), compared with 10.1% in the European, 8.8% in the African, 8.2% in the Eastern Mediterranean, and 6.8% in the America regions [5]. The Western Pacific and South-East Asian regions have seen a sharp increase in the prevalence of COPD in recent decades; in China alone, the Global Health Epidemiology Research Group estimated that there was an increase from an estimated 31 million cases in 1990 to 52 * Corresponding author. AstraZeneca, One MedImmune Way, Gaithersburg, MD, 20878, USA. E-mail address: Sami.Daoud@astrazeneca.com (S.Z. Daoud). Contents lists available at ScienceDirect Respiratory Medicine journal homepage: www.elsevier.com/locate/rmed https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rmed.2023.107393 Received 14 April 2023; Received in revised form 1 August 2023; Accepted 19 August 2023 Respiratory Medicine 218 (2023) 107393 2 million cases in 2010 [6] and, although the methodological approach was different, a systematic review [5] estimated there to be 105.8 million cases in 2019 [5]. Thus, the burden of COPD in Asia is substantial and continuing to grow [5–7]. However, although risk factors, including smoking, indoor pollutants, and socioeconomic status, among others, are known at the global level, a complete picture of the prevalence of, and risk factors for, COPD is not yet available in this region [8]. Combinations of long-acting muscarinic antagonists (LAMAs) and long-acting β2-agonists (LABAs) result in greater improvement of bronchodilation as well as increased symptom control, compared with monotherapies alone [1]. However, data regarding the efficacy and safety of LABA/LAMA combinations in patients from Asia are limited. The aim of this study was to evaluate aclidinium/formoterol and its mono-components in Asian patients with moderate-to-severe, stable COPD. 2. Objective To assess the efficacy and safety of aclidinium/formoterol vs monotherapies and aclidinium vs placebo when administered to patients from Asia with moderate-to-severe, stable COPD.

## Materials And Methods
3.1. Study design AVANT was a 24-week, Phase 3, randomized, parallel-group, double- blind, double-dummy study in patients with stable COPD (NCT03022097; Fig. 1). The first patient was enrolled February 2, 2017; the last patient last visit was April 14, 2022. Randomization was stratified by smoking status (current vs former smokers) and country (China, India, Philippines, Taiwan, and Vietnam). Patients were randomized 1:1:1:1 to aclidinium/formoterol 400/12 μg, aclidinium 400 μg, formoterol 12 μg, or placebo. Aclidinium/formoterol, aclidinium, and placebo were administered via the Genuair® dry powder inhaler (DPI) device. Formoterol and corresponding placebo were administered via the Turbuhaler® DPI device. The study was conducted according to the Declaration of Helsinki and received appropriate ethical approval. All patients provided written informed consent at the screening visit. 3.2. Patient population Eligible patients were aged ≥40 years, current or former smokers (≥10 pack-years smoking history), and had a diagnosis of stable moderate-to severe COPD (Stage II or III; post-bronchodilator forced expiratory volume in 1 s [FEV1] ≥30% and <80%, and post- bronchodilator FEV1/forced vital capacity [FVC] ratio <70%) at Visit 1 (screening) based on the American Thoracic Society/European Respiratory Society 2005 criteria [9] using normal values based on the Global Lung Function Initiative predicted values [10]. Patients were excluded if they had a history of or current diagnosis of asthma; a clinically significant respiratory condition other than COPD; and any respiratory tract infection or COPD exacerbation within 6 weeks prior to screening or during the run-in period. Vaccination against coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) during the study was permitted based on the benefits and risks for individual patients; it was recommended that patients were not to be randomized or undergo any study assessment within 7 days of receiving a COVID-19 vaccine. 3.3. Procedures A washout period for prohibited medication (oral, intra-nasal, or parenteral anticholinergic agents; LAMA; inhaled short-acting muscarnic antagonists [SAMA]; inhaled short-acting β2-agonists [SABA], LABA; LABA + ICS; SABA + SAMA; LABA + LAMA; methylxanthines; cromolyn sodium; nedocromil; leukotriene modifiers; phosphodiesterase type-IV inhibitors; continuous oral or parenteral corticosteroids equivalent to >10 mg prednisone daily or 20 mg every other day; non- selective β-blocking agents; and herbal or traditional medicines) was included prior to screening, with the duration varying from one day to one month, depending on the medication. Other medications, which were considered necessary for a patient’s safety and wellbeing, were given at the discretion of the Investigator, and recorded. Clinical visits occurred at screening (Week −2), Week 0, Week 1, Week 4, Week 12, Week 18, Week 24, and follow-up phone contact at Week 26 (Fig. 1). At the screening visit, medical and COPD histories were taken, along with spirometry, electrocardiogram (ECG), and physical examinations. Laboratory analyses were conducted, and COPD severity stage was assessed to obtain adequate data and evaluate study eligibility. A run-in period of 14 ± 3 days was conducted to assess disease stability in the absence of prohibited medications. At randomization (Week 0), patients were sequentially assigned a unique patient identification number, randomization code, and first medication kit number. Patients who discontinued treatment prematurely had an end-of- treatment visit and were invited to remain in the study. End-of-study was defined as the last visit of the last patient. 3.4. Endpoints The primary endpoints were change from baseline to Week 24 in (a) 1-h morning post-dose FEV1 (aclidinium/formoterol vs aclidinium; co- primary endpoint), (b) morning pre-dose (trough) FEV1 (aclidinium/ formoterol vs formoterol; co-primary endpoint), and (c) trough FEV1 (aclidinium vs placebo; primary endpoint). Morning pre-dose (trough) FEV1 was defined as the average of the corresponding −30- and 0-min timepoint values before the morning medication administration at Week 24. If data from one of these timepoints were missing, then the available data were used as the morning pre-dose value. Baseline was defined as the average of the two FEV1 values measured just prior to the administration of the first study medication dose at Week 0. Secondary endpoints included change from baseline to Week 24 in peak FEV1 (aclidinium vs placebo), and St George’s Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ) total scores (aclidinium/formoterol and aclidinium vs placebo) along with improvements in transition dyspnea index (TDI) focal score to Week 24 (aclidinium/formoterol and aclidinium vs placebo). Additional endpoints included onset of action (at 5 min), use of rescue medication (assessed at each timepoint), healthcare resource utiliztion (HCRU) and Exacerbations of Chronic Pulmonary Disease Tool (EXACT) COPD exacerbations, and EXACT-Respiratory Symptoms (E- RS) total score. Safety endpoints included treatment-emergent adverse events (AEs; non-serious AEs, serious AEs, and AEs of special interest, coded with Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities [version 24.1] terms), clinical laboratory tests, blood pressure, 12-lead ECGs, and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE; an adjudicated composite of the total of cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, and non- fatal stroke). 3.5. Statistical analysis A sample of 1060 patients (265 per group) was estimated to provide ≥90% power to detect statistically significant differences at Week 24 in (a) change from baseline in 1-h morning post-dose FEV1 of 100 mL (aclidinium/formoterol vs aclidinium; standard deviation [SD] 230 mL), (b) change from baseline in morning pre-dose (trough) FEV1 of 65 mL (aclidinium/formoterol vs formoterol; SD 230 mL), (c) change from baseline in trough FEV1 of 100 mL (aclidinium vs placebo; SD 230 mL), and (d) change from baseline in peak FEV1 of 175 mL (aclidinium vs placebo; SD 230 mL). In addition, this sample size was estimated to provide ≥90% power for TDI and SGRQ. All tests were performed using 2-sided tests at the 5% significance level. The analysis of all efficacy endpoints was performed using the intent-to-treat population (all randomized patients who took ≥1 dose of study medication and had at least a baseline FEV1, regardless of adherence to the randomized treatment), except for COPD exacerbations, which were analyzed for the safety population (actual treatment). The estimand was based on a ‘while on treatment’ approach where treatment estimates were based on the on-treatment period while patients were taking the study medication (up to the time of withdrawal or completion); exacerbations were based on both on-treatment and treatment policy estimands (on-study data, regardless of treatment). Primary and secondary variables were analyzed by mixed models for repeated measures. Common fixed-effect factors were treatment group, country, smoking status, visit, and treatment group-by-visit interaction. In addition, for morning post-dose, trough, and peak FEV1, the following baseline covariates were included: pre- and post-bronchodilator (salbutamol) FEV1 at screening, age, and baseline FEV1; and for TDI and SGRQ, the corresponding baseline value (baseline dyspnea index or SGRQ) and age. Missing data were not imputed. The estimated mean (least squares [LS] mean) for each treatment and the estimated mean difference for each pairwise treatment comparison at all study visits were extracted from treatment-by-visit interaction in the model along with their standard errors and two-sided 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and the p-values corresponding to the between-treatment group differences. A hierarchical testing approach was implemented to control for multiplicity for primary and secondary efficacy endpoints (Supplemental Table S1); statistical comparisons outside this approach are thus referred to as nominal. Demographic and other baseline characteristics, as well as safety parameters, were analyzed in the safety population (defined as all randomized patients who took ≥1 dose of study medication). Safety results are presented as descriptive statistics across time and treatment groups. The rate of COPD exacerbations per years of exposure was analyzed by means of negative binomial regression models including age as a covariate, and baseline ICS use (use/no use of ICS as monotherapy within 15 days prior to the first dose and continued after randomization), baseline COPD severity (mild/moderate vs severe/very severe), smoking status (current/former smokers), country, prior history of exacerbation over 12 months before randomization (yes/no), and treatment group as factors, and the log risk time in years as an offset. Treatment effects and pairwise treatment comparisons were estimated by the adjusted event rates per patient-year and the rate ratio on the treatment coefficient, respectively.

## Results

## Discussion
In this study in patients from Asia with moderate-to-severe, stable COPD, treatment with aclidinium provided higher bronchodilation compared with placebo and, moreover, aclidinium/formoterol provided higher bronchodilation compared with aclidinium and formoterol. This was evidenced by change from baseline to Week 24 in 1-h morning post- dose FEV1, in morning pre-dose (trough) FEV1, and/or in peak FEV1. Aclidinium/formoterol demonstrated rapid onset of action, with an improvement in FEV1 vs placebo on Day 1 at 5 min post-dose. Improvements in TDI focal score by Week 24 were observed in patients treated with aclidinium/formoterol, compared with placebo. Improvements in SGRQ by Week 24 were observed in patients treated with aclidinium/formoterol or aclidinium, compared with placebo. Moreover, improvements in HCRU COPD exacerbation rate (any severity) and E-RS total score were observed for both aclidinium/formoterol and aclidinium vs placebo. Finally, change from baseline over 24 weeks in use of rescue medication was greater with aclidinium/formoterol vs placebo but not with aclidinium vs placebo. In terms of safety, aclidinium/formoterol and aclidinium were well tolerated and safety findings were consistent with the known profiles. The overall results in patients from Asia are in alignment with those of the similarly designed, global, AUGMENT, ACLIFORM, and AMPLIFY studies in patients with COPD, which showed that treatment with aclidinium/formoterol resulted in sustained and clinically meaningful improvements vs monotherapies and placebo, with a safety profile consistent with that already established [11–13]. The results are also broadly consistent with the results of several other studies of treatments now approved in China. In the IGNITE clinical trial program, improvements in lung function were observed following treatment with indacaterol/glycopyrronium compared with placebo, monotherapies, tiotropium, salmeterol/fluticasone, and/or tiotropium/formoterol, with a favorable safety and tolerability profile [14]. In the KRONOS study, improvements in lung function were observed with budesonide/glycopyrronium/formoterol triple therapy vs glycopyrronium/formoterol and budesonide/formoterol, with a safety and tolerability profile consistent with those of the dual comparators [15]. Finally, in the PINNACLE 4 study, improved lung function was observed with glycopyrronium/formoterol vs monotherapies and placebo, with a safety profile similar to LABAs [16]. The efficacy and safety of aclidinium/formoterol in Asian patients with moderate-to-severe, stable COPD appeared similar to that of other ethnic/regional groups. This is consistent with the findings of several other LABA/LAMA combination studies conducted partly or completely in Asia. The TONADO studies of another LABA/LAMA combination found that after 24 weeks, FEV1 exposure response, and trough FEV1 responses were greater with tiotropium/olodaterol vs monotherapy and were consistent across global and East Asian populations, with no increase in AEs among East Asian patients [17]. In the TRIVERSYTI study in patients from East Asia (82% of whom were from China), the difference in pre-dose and 2-h post-dose FEV1 between each treatment group (extrafine beclomethasone dipropionate/formoterol/glycopyrronium vs Table 2 Incidence of treatment-emergent adverse events (safety population). n (%) AB/FF (n = 263) AB (n = 266) FF (n = 264) Placebo (n = 269) Any AE 144 (54.8) 126 (47.4) 141 (53.4) 145 (53.9) Any AE (mild) 108 (41.1) 90 (33.8) 93 (35.2) 111 (41.3) Any AE (moderate) 56 (21.3) 55 (20.7) 63 (23.9) 56 (20.8) Any AE (severe) 16 (6.1) 14 (5.3) 20 (7.6) 16 (5.9) Any AE related to study medication 24 (9.1) 18 (6.8) 9 (3.4) 17 (6.3) Any AE leading to death 0 0 1 (0.4) 2 (0.7) Any SAE 19 (7.2) 21 (7.9) 26 (9.8) 21 (7.8) Any AE leading to discontinuation 6 (2.3) 4 (1.5) 5 (1.9) 6 (2.2) Most commonly reported AEsa COPD exacerbation 32 (12.2) 26 (9.8) 42 (15.9) 41 (15.2) URTI 31 (11.8) 26 (9.8) 24 (9.1) 24 (8.9) Nasopharyngitis 7 (2.7) 5 (1.9) 11 (4.2) 5 (1.9) Cough 7 (2.7) 2 (0.8) 3 (1.1) 13 (4.8) Back pain 6 (2.3) 2 (0.8) 4 (1.5) 2 (0.7) Any AE of special interest 52 (19.8) 50 (18.8) 49 (18.6) 73 (27.1) Cardiac and cerebrovascular 17 (6.5) 12 (4.5) 11 (4.2) 19 (7.1) Any treatment- emergent adjudicated MACE 0 2 (0.8) 2 (0.8) 4 (1.5) Anticholinergic 20 (7.6) 15 (5.6) 13 (4.9) 26 (9.7) β2 adrenergic 36 (13.7) 31 (11.7) 33 (12.5) 51 (19.0) Pneumonia 3 (1.1) 5 (1.9) 9 (3.4) 7 (2.6) n = number of patients. In a subgroup analysis of Chinese participants in the KRONOS study, budesonide/glycopyrrolate/formoterol provided benefits in terms of lung function, symptoms, and exacerbations vs dual therapies (glycopyrrolate/formoterol, budesonide/formoterol, or budesonide/formoterol), and findings were generally consistent with the KRONOS global population [20]. The safety profile was also consistent between the Chinese and global KRONOS populations, reflecting the findings of a previous pharmacokinetic study [21]. The initiation of bronchodilator monotherapy or combination therapy for COPD varies based on local guidelines. The GOLD 2015 [22] guidelines are the most widely used and state that patients with stable COPD may be started on single or dual long-acting bronchodilator therapy, even though combination LABA/LAMA treatment increases FEV1, reduces symptoms, and reduces exacerbation frequency compared with monotherapy [1]. Although Chinese guidelines are similar to GOLD, guidelines for Australia, Japan, and Korea use a step-wise approach to optimize pharmacotherapy for stable COPD, and state that when monotherapy is not sufficiently successful then combination LABA/LAMA treatment should be used [23]. Taiwanese guidelines state that for patients with mild symptoms, and a low risk of acute exacerbation, single LABA- or LAMA-based bronchodilator therapy is recommended as first-line treatment [24]. If patients experience inadequate control of symptoms or repeated exacerbations after bronchodilator monotherapy, fixed-dose dual bronchodilator therapy (LABA/LAMA) can be considered. In contrast, for patients with severe initial symptoms, fixed-dose dual bronchodilator therapy is recommended as a first-line therapy. Of note, in this study, COPD was classified as severe in approximately half of patients (mean post-dose FEV1 was approximately 50% of predicted, and 35% of patients had experienced COPD exacerbations in the prior 12 months). It is therefore clear that alignment of guidelines across different regions would allow for a more consistent approach to treatment; efficacy and safety outcomes of the AVANT study could contribute to the development of such guidelines. Strengths of this study include our finding of similar efficacy and safety outcomes in patients in Asia — with the majority of individuals originating from China — compared with global studies. Moreover, the incidence of MACE was similar in the Asian population to that observed in global studies, including those conducted in the US, which has a diverse population. This is of particular interest, as South Asian populations generally exhibit a higher prevalence and earlier onset of cardiovascular complications compared with other populations [25]. The study has some limitations. The study was conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic, which resulted in some disruption to the rate of enrollment; however, we did not observe any impact of the pandemic on individual patient data or treatment compliance. In a survey of COPD management during the early period of the pandemic in Beijing, most patients (75.2%) maintained their usual pharmaceutical treatment as they had prior to the pandemic (81.7%) [26]. In addition, the large majority of patients in the study population were male, which may limit comparability with data from other studies in different regions. However, this population is reflective of the lower prevalence of COPD among females in China [27], which is largely explained by smoking behaviors. With regard to exacerbations, non-pharmacologic interventions during the COVID-19 pandemic meant that patients spent much more time at home, where the environment was controlled and exposure to exacerbation triggers was greatly limited. Additionally, there may have been underreporting of symptoms/mild exacerbations due to fewer study visits and interactions with the study site where patients would otherwise have been retrained to report rescue medication use, symptoms etc. Finally, this study was not powered for the evaluation of exacerbation rates between treatment groups.

## Conclusions
In patients from Asia with moderate-to-severe, stable COPD, aclidinium provided clinically meaningful bronchodilation vs placebo while aclidinium/formoterol provided higher bronchodilation than monotherapies. In addition, while improvements in symptoms and quality of life were observed with aclidinium, those improvements were clinically meaningful for aclidinium/formoterol compared with placebo. Moreover, aclidinium/formoterol was well tolerated, with comparable rates of treatment-emergent AEs across treatment groups. Thus, the results of this study extend the existing knowledge about aclidinium/formoterol and aclidinium to the Asian population.

title: Effects of MIdazolam versus MOrphine in acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: An analysis of MIMO trial.
body:
AIMS: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is an important comorbidity in heart failure. The MIMO trial showed that patients with acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema (ACPE) treated with midazolam had fewer serious adverse events than those treated with morphine. In this post hoc analysis, we examined whether the presence/ absence of COPD modifies the reduced risk of midazolam over morphine.
METHODS: Patients >18 years old clinically diagnosed with ACPE and with dyspnea and anxiety were randomized (1:1) at emergency department arrival to receive either intravenous midazolam or morphine. In this post hoc analysis, we calculated the relative risk (RR) of serious adverse events in patients with and without COPD. Calculating the CochranMantel-Haenszel interaction test, we evaluated if COPD modified the reduced risk of serious adverse events in the midazolam arm compared to morphine.
RESULTS: Overall, 25 (22.5%) of the 111 patients randomized had a history of COPD. Patients with COPD were more commonly men with a history of previous episodes of heart failure, than participants without COPD. In the COPD group, the RR for the incidence of serious adverse events in the midazolam versus morphine arm was 0.36 (95%CI, 0.1-1.46). In the group without COPD, the RR was 0.44 (95%CI, 0.22-0.91). The presence of COPD did not modify the reduced risk of serious adverse events in the midazolam arm compared to morphine (p for interaction =0.79).
CONCLUSIONS: The reduced risk of serious adverse events in the midazolam group compared with morphine is similar in patients with and without COPD.
